title: Grit test: how gritty are you? Free grit scale quiz — cv.cm
description: Free grit test: rate 14 statements about perseverance and sticking with long-term goals to get a score from 0 to 56, what it means and how to build grit. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
h1: Grit test: how gritty are you?
lede: Do you finish what you start, or drop goals when the next shiny idea comes along? Rate 14 statements to see how much grit, passion plus perseverance for long-term goals, you bring to work, study and life.
about: Grit is a term made popular by psychologist Angela Duckworth for the mix of passion and perseverance that keeps people working toward long-term goals for years, through setbacks and boredom. In her research, grit predicted who would stay the course at a military academy or go further in a national spelling bee, alongside talent. Later studies found grit overlaps a lot with conscientiousness and matters less than early headlines suggested, but sticking with goals you care about still makes a real difference.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the two sides of grit: perseverance (keeping going after setbacks) and consistency of interest (staying with the same goals). They are not the Grit Scale or any other published questionnaire, and half of them describe the opposite, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. The score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs.

faq.a: Passion and perseverance for long-term goals: staying with something you care about for a long time and keeping going when it gets hard.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 is in the middle and 38 or more is high.
Yes. Duckworth suggests finding goals that interest you, practicing deliberately, connecting your work to a purpose and treating setbacks as part of learning. A growth mindset helps too.
No. Sometimes quitting is the wise choice, when a goal no longer fits you or costs your health. Grit works best for goals you truly care about.

items: When I commit to something, I see it through to the end.
I often drop a project as soon as a more exciting one comes along.
A failure makes me try harder rather than give up.
I change my main goals every year or two.
I'll keep practicing a skill for months to get good at it.
What I want to achieve seems to shift all the time.
I have been working toward the same big goal for a long time.
Once the novelty wears off, I tend to lose interest.
I put in steady effort even when the work is dull.
Long projects make me restless before they're finished.
If one approach fails, I look for another way in.
Slow progress usually makes me want to quit.
The things I care most about haven't changed in years.
Starting something new appeals to me more than finishing what I've started.

low.name: Low grit (0–18)
low.body: Right now you tend to switch goals or step back when things get hard or dull. That can mean you're still exploring, which is fine. To build grit, pick one goal you really care about, break it into small steps, and keep going for a set time, say a month, before you decide whether to change course.

mid.name: Moderate grit (19–37)
mid.body: You stick with some goals but not others, probably depending on how much they interest you. That's normal. Notice what keeps you going on the goals you finish, such as a clear purpose, a routine or a friend to report to, and use it on the ones you tend to drop.

high.name: High grit (38–56)
high.body: You keep going after setbacks and stay with long-term goals, which is a real strength at work, in study and in life. Keep checking that your goals still matter to you, rest so that your perseverance lasts, and remember that quitting the wrong goal can be a smart move too.
